chapter_theme: The ten of knowing (அறிவுப் பத்து) names, line by line, the outward sign by which a hidden quality is recognised: great or small birth by kindness or pride, kindness by giving, friendship by help, learning by discernment, theft by trickery, all lapses by a lapse of speech or understanding, and ability by deeds.

11.reading: Birth into a great house is said to be recognised by the kindness, the moistness of heart, a person shows.
11.nuance: Line 1 is the frame that heads every ten; the saying is line 2. ஈரம், literally moisture, is the softness of heart that the next line ties to giving, so the two lines make a chain. பேரில் (பேர் இல், a great house) ranks families, but the test it names is conduct, not descent.

norm.note: a claim of the period that a great house of birth shows itself in the conduct of those born to it

items.claim: birth in a great house is known by one's kindness

12.reading: Possessing kindness is said to be recognised by one's giving.
12.nuance: The inner quality is read only through the outward act: a feeling that does not give is not counted as kindness.

items.claim: the possession of kindness is known by giving

13.reading: A good friendship that does not fail is said to be recognised by the help given in it.
13.nuance: Our text reads சேரா, 'not joined'; tamilvu reads சோரா, 'not slackening', which gives the plain sense followed here. With சேரா the line would speak of the good friendship of those not joined by kin, which is possible but strained.

items.claim: an unfailing good friendship is known by the help it gives

14.reading: Having learned is said to be recognised by one's power of seeing, the discernment learning gives.
14.nuance: காட்சி can be insight or judgment, and less likely outward bearing; on either reading learning is proved by what the learner perceives, not by what he recites.

items.claim: having learned is known by one's discernment

15.reading: Eminence is said to be recognised by the way one goes forward to meet and receive others, or by how one meets an encounter.
15.nuance: எதிர்கொளின் (tamilvu எதிர்கோளின்) is either the courteous going out to receive a guest or superior, or the facing of an opponent or trial. The first fits the ten's run of social virtues; the line does not decide.

items.claim: eminence is known by one's going forward to receive, or by one's meeting of an encounter

16.reading: Birth in a small house is said to be recognised by swagger and pride.
16.nuance: This is the mirror of line 11: the great house shows in kindness, the small house in பெருமிதம். சிற்றில் may mean a mean or poor family rather than a birth-group; either way the line reads a family's rank from a fault of conduct.

norm.note: a claim of the period that low birth shows in arrogant conduct

items.claim: birth in a small house is known by arrogance

17.reading: Being a thief is said to be recognised from the doing of trickery.
17.nuance: குத்திரம் is fraud or a crooked trick, not theft itself: the line calls a man a thief from the deceit in his acts before any goods are taken.

items.claim: being a thief is known by working deceit

18.reading: From a lapse in speech, every other lapse a person has is said to be recognised.
18.nuance: Here the order of the ten turns: what is known (எச்சோர்வும், every lapse) comes after its sign. The item is the thing known, read with the sign சொற்சோர்வு.

items.claim: every lapse is known from a slip in speech

19.reading: From a lapse in understanding, the other lapses too are said to be recognised.
19.nuance: Built on the same frame as line 18, it moves the telling lapse from the tongue to the mind; the two lines together make speech and understanding the two places where all failing shows.

items.claim: other lapses are known from a lapse of understanding

20.reading: Excellent manly ability is said to be recognised by what one actually does.
20.nuance: The ten closes on deeds: after birth, kindness, friendship and learning, the last test is performance.

items.claim: excellent manly ability is known by deeds

links.note: Line 11 reads great birth from kindness; line 12 reads kindness from giving.
links.teaches: Taken in order the two lines make a chain of evidence, so in this ten noble birth is finally proved by the act of giving.

links.note: Line 11 says a great house shows in kindness; line 16 says a small house shows in pride.
links.teaches: The pair shows the ten treating rank of birth as real yet legible only in conduct, with kindness and pride as its two marks.

links.note: Kural 959 reads lineage from a person's speech; the line reads great birth from kindness.
links.teaches: Both read birth from a sign, but the sign moves from what is said to what is felt, so the Muthumozhikkanchi's test is harder to counterfeit.
links.list_adds: Set in a ten of signs, the line makes kindness the test of birth and the next line makes giving the test of kindness, a chain the couplet does not build.

links.note: Kural 796 says ruin is the rod that measures one's people; the line names help as the mark of a friendship that does not fail.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the occasion of the test and the line gives its measure, so together they say what ruin reveals: who still helps.
links.list_adds: It places the friendship test among tests of birth, learning and ability, so friendship is judged by the same rule of outward proof as every other claimed virtue.

links.note: Thirikadugam 37 says the extent of friendship shows in backbiting; the line says a good friendship shows in help.
links.teaches: The two give friendship a positive and a negative test, help given and slander withheld, so neither alone measures it.

links.note: Kural 717 says learning shines among those who can examine words; the line says learning is known by the learner's own discernment.
links.teaches: The Kural needs a qualified audience for learning to appear, while the line finds the proof inside the learner, in how he sees.
links.list_adds: By setting learning between friendship and eminence in a run of signs, it treats learning as one more inner fact read from outward evidence rather than as display before an assembly.

links.note: Kural 978 says smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; the line says birth in a small house shows in pride.
links.teaches: The same mark of pride serves the Kural as a sign of small character and the Muthumozhikkanchi as a sign of small birth, which shows the ten tying character to family.
links.list_adds: Paired in the ten with line 11, it sets the small house against the great one, a contrast of birth the couplet, which speaks only of character, does not draw.

links.note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are only words and that lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort; the line treats a small house of birth as a fact that pride reveals.
links.teaches: Read together they show two answers in one group: the Naladiyar dissolves birth rank into achievement, while the Muthumozhikkanchi keeps rank and reads it from conduct.
links.list_adds: Its pairing with line 11 sets great and small houses as fixed ranks with opposite marks, which is exactly the distinction the quatrain calls empty words.

links.note: Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge absent in those who love measure; the line names trickery as what shows a man to be a thief.
links.teaches: The Kural places theft in a kind of cunning, and the line turns that cunning into the evidence, so the thief is known by his method before any taking.
links.list_adds: Among signs of good birth, kindness and learning, it gives the one sign of a crime, so the ten's method of reading people from acts reaches the detection of a thief.

links.note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin come from speech and bids one guard against its lapse; the line says a lapse in speech reveals every other lapse.
links.teaches: The Kural treats a slip of the tongue as a cause of loss, while the line treats it as evidence, so the guarded tongue both protects and conceals.
links.list_adds: Set beside line 19, it makes speech and understanding the two windows through which all other failings are seen, a pairing the couplet lacks.

links.note: Lines 18 and 19 share one frame: a lapse in one place reveals lapses elsewhere, first in speech and then in understanding.
links.teaches: The repeated frame shows the ten holding that faults do not stay single: one visible slip is read as the index of hidden ones.

links.note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool and inner fortress that guards against faults; the line says a lapse of understanding exposes the other lapses.
links.teaches: Read together, the fortress image explains the line: once understanding gives way, the faults it guarded behind it come into view.
links.list_adds: It moves understanding from a guard to a sign, placing its failure among the ten's ways of reading a person.

links.note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the single touchstone of greatness and smallness; the line makes deeds the test of manly ability only.
links.teaches: The Kural uses one test for all worth, while this ten assigns a different sign to each quality, kindness for birth and giving for kindness, and keeps deeds for ability.
links.list_adds: As the last of ten paired signs, it shows deeds as one test among several, each matched to its quality, rather than the one touchstone the couplet names.

source_issues: 11 line 2: the comparison site's text lacks this line; the shared frame line 1 is printed with verse 11 here and the saying is line 2.
13 line 1: our text reads சேரா; tamilvu reads சோரா (e/o vowel sign), which gives the plainer sense 'unfailing'. The (பு) in நல்நட்(பு) is an editorial restoration.
15 line 1: tamilvu reads ஏற்றம் உடைமை எதிர்கோளின் for ஏற்ற முடைமை எதிர்கொளின் (word division and e/o vowel sign).
